title: Food as Fuel
bigQuestion: How can food from many places give your body what it needs to grow, learn and play?

story.title: Five Lunches, One Table
story.kicker: A class learns that healthy lunches look very different around the world.
paragraphs: Ms. Rivera's fifth-grade class has a new project. Each group gets a photo of a school lunch from another country. Their job is to find out what is on the tray. Then they will compare all five lunches.

Group one has a lunch from Japan. There is rice, a piece of fish, cooked greens and soup. Group two has a lunch from Brazil. There is rice, black beans, a little meat and a salad. The students notice rice in both.

Group three looks at a lunch from India. There is lentil dal, rice, a flatbread and cooked vegetables. Group four has a lunch from China, with noodles and stir-fried vegetables. Group five has a lunch from the United States, with a turkey sandwich, carrots, an apple and milk.

The class lays the photos side by side. Jamal says, "They all look so different." Priya says, "But they all have a grain, a vegetable and something with protein." Ms. Rivera smiles. Priya has found the big idea.
There is no one right lunch for the whole world. Families eat many different foods. Healthy eating is about balance and variety. The class decides to learn what each food gives the body.
story.think: Which of the five lunches would you most like to try? What parts does it share with a lunch you eat at home?

lessons.title: Carbohydrates for Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Carbohydrates are the body's main source of energy, and whole grains give steady energy.
reading: Food gives your body things it needs. These are called *nutrients*. There are six main kinds: carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals and water. Each one has its own job.

*Carbohydrates* are your body's main fuel. They are in rice, bread, pasta, tortillas, fruit, beans and potatoes. Your body turns them into a sugar that your cells burn for energy. Your brain uses a lot of it.

Some grains are *whole grains*, like brown rice, oatmeal and whole-wheat bread. They keep the outer part of the grain. That part has fiber. Fiber helps food move through your intestines and helps you feel full longer.

words.d: the things in food that the body needs to grow, move and stay healthy
nutrients in grains, fruits and beans that are the body's main fuel
grains that keep their outer part, like brown rice and oatmeal

look.title: Energy in One Gram
look.cite: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Nutrition Facts label guidance
look.prompt: Which nutrient packs the most energy into one gram? About how many times more than carbohydrate?

check.q: What is the main job of carbohydrates?
check.why: The reading says carbohydrates are the body's main fuel.

check.q: Which food is a whole grain?
check.why: Oatmeal is a whole grain. It keeps the outer part of the grain, which has fiber.

check.q: How does fiber help you?
choices: It helps food move through the intestines
It is a kind of vitamin
It makes the heart beat faster
check.why: The reading says fiber helps food move through your intestines and helps you feel full.

lessons.title: Protein Builds
lessons.mainIdea: Protein helps the body build and repair muscles, skin and other parts.
reading: A scraped knee heals in a week or two. New skin grows over the cut. To build that skin, your body uses *protein*. Protein is a nutrient that builds and repairs body parts.

Protein comes from many foods. Fish, chicken, eggs, milk and meat have protein. So do plant foods like beans, lentils, tofu, peanuts and seeds. Rice and beans together are a protein-rich meal eaten in many countries.
Your muscles, skin, hair and nails are built with protein. Growing children need protein every day. Eating it from different foods is a good way to get enough.

words.d: a nutrient that helps the body build and repair muscles, skin and other parts
small, flat seeds from a plant in the bean family, often cooked into soups and dal

look.title: Protein Hunt
look.text: Look back at the five lunches. Japan had fish. Brazil had black beans and a little meat. India had lentil dal. The United States had turkey and milk. China had noodles and vegetables, and some stir-fries add tofu or egg.
look.prompt: Find the protein on each tray. Which ones come from plants, and which come from animals?

check.q: What does protein do for the body?
choices: It builds and repairs body parts
It is the main fuel for the brain
It keeps water out of the body
check.why: The reading says protein builds and repairs body parts, like new skin over a cut.

check.q: Which is a plant food with protein?
check.why: Lentils, beans, tofu, peanuts and seeds are plant foods with protein.

check.q: Which body parts are built with protein?
check.why: The reading lists muscles, skin, hair and nails as parts built with protein.

lessons.title: Fats Help Too
lessons.mainIdea: The body needs some fat for energy and health, and fats from plants and fish are good choices.
reading: Some people think all fat is bad. That is not true. Your body needs some *fat*. Fat stores energy. It helps your body use some vitamins. It also helps build your brain and nerves.
Fats come in different kinds. Olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocados and fish have fats that are good for the heart. These are often called *healthy fats*.
Butter, cheese and fatty meats have another kind of fat. It is fine in small amounts. Fried snacks and many sweets have a lot of fat and sugar. Doctors say to enjoy them sometimes, not every day.

words.d: a nutrient that stores energy and helps the body use some vitamins
fats from foods like olive oil, nuts, avocados and fish that are good for the heart

look.title: Two Snacks
look.text: Snack A is a handful of peanuts and an orange. Snack B is a bag of fried chips. Both have fat. The peanuts also bring protein. The orange brings vitamins and water.
look.prompt: Which snack gives the body more kinds of nutrients? Is it still okay to enjoy chips sometimes? Explain.

check.q: Which statement about fat is true?
choices: All fat is bad for you
check.why: The reading says your body needs some fat to store energy, use vitamins and build the brain.

check.q: Which food has healthy fats?
check.why: Olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocados and fish have fats that are good for the heart.

check.q: What do doctors say about fried snacks and sweets?
choices: Enjoy them sometimes, not every day
They are the best source of protein
check.why: The reading says to enjoy them sometimes, not every day.

lessons.title: Vitamins and Minerals
lessons.mainIdea: Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts, and colorful foods help you get many of them.
reading: Long ago, sailors on long trips got very sick. Their gums bled and they felt weak. In the 1700s, a Scottish doctor named James Lind tested different foods. The sailors who ate oranges and lemons got better. Today we know those fruits have *vitamin* C.

Vitamins are nutrients your body needs in small amounts. Vitamin C helps heal cuts. Vitamin A, in carrots and sweet potatoes, helps your eyes. Vitamin D helps your bones. Your skin makes some vitamin D in sunlight.

*Minerals* come from the earth and get into plants and animals. Calcium, in milk, yogurt, tofu and leafy greens, builds strong bones and teeth. Iron, in beans, spinach and meat, helps blood carry oxygen. Eating many colors of fruits and vegetables helps you get many vitamins and minerals.

words.d: a nutrient the body needs in small amounts to work well
nutrients from the earth, like calcium and iron, that the body needs
a mineral that builds strong bones and teeth

look.title: James Lind's Test
look.text: Twelve sailors with scurvy were split into pairs, and each pair was given a different extra food. The two who ate oranges and lemons got better the fastest. One was fit for duty in about six days.
look.cite: James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy, 1753 (retold in plain words)
look.prompt: How was Lind's test fair? Why did he give each pair a different food?

check.q: Which fruits helped James Lind's sailors?
check.why: The sailors who ate oranges and lemons got better. These fruits have vitamin C.

check.q: Which mineral builds strong bones and teeth?
check.why: The reading says calcium builds strong bones and teeth.

check.q: What is one simple way to get many vitamins and minerals?
choices: Eat many colors of fruits and vegetables
check.why: The reading says eating many colors of fruits and vegetables helps you get many vitamins and minerals.

lessons.title: Water Keeps You Going
lessons.mainIdea: Water is a nutrient too; it makes up much of your body and helps every system work.
reading: After gym class, your mouth feels dry. You head to the drinking fountain. Your body is asking for *water*. Water is one of the six nutrients. You can live much longer without food than without water.
Much of your body is water. It is in your blood, your muscles and even your bones. Water carries nutrients to your cells. It helps you digest food. It helps make sweat to cool you down.

You lose water all day when you breathe, sweat and use the bathroom. So you need to drink more. Plain water and milk are good choices. Fruits like watermelon and oranges have water too. Feeling thirsty is a sign your body needs water; being low on water is called being *dehydrated*.

words.d: a nutrient that carries food to cells, helps digestion and keeps the body cool
when the body does not have enough water

look.title: How Much of You Is Water?
look.cite: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School, The Water in You
look.prompt: Who has a higher share of water, a baby or an adult? Which body part on the list has the most?

check.q: What does being dehydrated mean?
choices: Not having enough water in the body
check.why: The reading says being low on water is called being dehydrated.

check.q: Which is one job of water in the body?
choices: It is the body's main fuel
check.why: The reading says water carries nutrients to your cells and helps with digestion and sweat.

check.q: According to the U.S. Geological Survey, about how much of an adult's body is water?
check.why: The data table from the USGS shows an adult body is about 60 percent water.

lessons.title: MyPlate
lessons.mainIdea: MyPlate shows a balanced meal: half fruits and vegetables, plus grains, protein and dairy.
reading: Picture a dinner plate cut into four parts, with a small cup beside it. This picture is called *MyPlate*. The U.S. Department of Agriculture made it in 2011 to help families plan meals.

On MyPlate, fruits and vegetables fill half the plate. Grains fill about a quarter. Protein foods fill the last quarter. The cup stands for dairy, like milk or yogurt. Soy milk with added calcium counts too.

MyPlate is a guide, not a strict rule. It works with foods from any culture. A bowl of rice with fish and greens fits. So do beans, tortillas and salsa. The idea is *balance*: some of each group over the day.

words.d: a U.S. picture guide that shows a balanced meal as a plate with food groups
eating some of each food group, not too much of just one
milk and foods made from milk, like yogurt and cheese

look.title: The MyPlate Message
look.text: Make half your plate fruits and vegetables. Make half your grains whole grains. Vary your protein foods. Move to low-fat or fat-free milk or yogurt, or fortified soy versions.
look.cite: U.S. Department of Agriculture, MyPlate, 2011 (tips in plain words)
look.prompt: Pick one tip. What is one small change a family could make at dinner to follow it?

check.q: On MyPlate, how much of the plate is fruits and vegetables?
check.why: The reading says fruits and vegetables fill half the plate.

check.q: What does the cup next to the plate stand for?
check.why: The cup stands for dairy, like milk or yogurt, or fortified soy milk.

check.q: Which statement about MyPlate is true?
choices: It only works for American foods
It says to eat just one food group
It works with foods from any culture
check.why: The reading says MyPlate is a guide that works with foods from any culture. It was made in 2011.

lessons.title: Reading a Food Label
lessons.mainIdea: The Nutrition Facts label tells you the serving size and what nutrients are in a packaged food.
reading: Pick up a box of cereal and turn it around. You will find a white box with black letters. It is called the *Nutrition Facts* label. Most packaged foods in the United States must have one.

Start at the top. Find the *serving size*. This is the amount the numbers are about, like one cup. If you eat two cups, you get twice as much of everything. Next, find calories. Calories tell how much energy the food gives.

Then look down the list. You will see fat, sodium, carbohydrates, fiber, sugars and protein. The label also shows added sugars. Added sugars are sugars put in when the food is made. The right side shows a *percent Daily Value*. As a rough guide, 5 percent is low and 20 percent is high.

words.d: the label on packaged food that lists its nutrients
the amount of food that the label's numbers describe
a number on the label that shows if a food is low or high in a nutrient

look.title: Two Cereals
look.text: Cereal A: serving size 1 cup, 3 grams of fiber, 12 grams of added sugars. Cereal B: serving size 1 cup, 5 grams of fiber, 4 grams of added sugars. Both boxes show the same serving size.
look.prompt: Which cereal has more fiber and fewer added sugars? Why does it matter that the serving sizes are the same?

check.q: What does the serving size tell you?
choices: The amount the label's numbers are about
check.why: The serving size is the amount of food that all the label's numbers describe.

check.q: About what percent Daily Value is thought of as high?
check.why: The reading gives a rough guide: 5 percent is low and 20 percent is high.

check.q: If you eat two servings, what happens to the numbers?
choices: You get twice as much of everything
check.why: The label's numbers are for one serving. Two servings means twice as much.

lessons.title: Sugar and Your Teeth
lessons.mainIdea: Germs in the mouth use sugar to make acid that can harm teeth, so brushing and fewer sugary drinks help.
reading: Your teeth are covered in *enamel*. Enamel is the hardest part of your body. But tiny germs live in every mouth. When you eat sugar, the germs eat it too. They make acid. Over time, acid can make holes in teeth called *cavities*.

Sticky candy and sugary drinks are hardest on teeth. Soda, sweet tea and juice wash sugar over teeth again and again. Water is a great drink for your teeth. The World Health Organization advises that people keep added sugars low.

You can help your teeth every day. Brush two times a day with fluoride toothpaste. Fluoride is a mineral that makes enamel stronger. See a dentist for checkups. A sweet treat now and then is fine, especially with a meal.

words.d: the hard, shiny outer layer of a tooth
holes in teeth made by acid from germs
a mineral in toothpaste and many water supplies that makes enamel stronger

look.title: Advice on Sugar
look.text: Adults and children should get less than 10 percent of their daily energy from free sugars, which are sugars added to food and drink plus the sugar in honey, syrups and juice. Going below 5 percent may bring even more benefit.
look.cite: World Health Organization, Guideline: Sugars Intake for Adults and Children, 2015 (plain-words summary)
look.prompt: Name two drinks from your week that have free sugars. What could you drink instead?

check.q: What makes cavities in teeth?
choices: Acid made by germs that eat sugar
check.why: The reading says germs eat sugar and make acid, and acid can make holes called cavities.

check.q: What does fluoride do?
check.why: Fluoride is a mineral that makes enamel stronger.

check.q: Which drink is best for your teeth?
check.why: The reading says water is a great drink for your teeth. Sugary drinks wash sugar over teeth.

lessons.title: Healthy Foods Around the World
lessons.mainIdea: Families around the world eat many different healthy meals that give the body the same kinds of nutrients.
reading: In Brazil and Mexico, many families eat *rice and beans*. The rice gives carbohydrates. The beans give protein and fiber. Eaten together, they make a filling, healthy meal.

In India, many families eat *dal*. Dal is a warm stew of lentils cooked with spices like turmeric and cumin. It is often served with rice or flatbread. In China, families often stir-fry vegetables in a hot pan with a little oil.

In Japan and many coastal places, people eat a lot of fish. Fish gives protein and healthy fats. Each culture has its own foods. Many of them fit MyPlate well. You can enjoy your family's foods and try new ones too.

words.d: a meal eaten in many countries that gives carbohydrates, protein and fiber
a warm stew of lentils and spices common in India
to cook small pieces of food quickly in a hot pan with a little oil

look.title: Match the Plate
look.text: A plate from Mexico: rice, black beans, grilled chicken, salsa and a slice of avocado. A plate from India: rice, lentil dal, spinach cooked with spices and a spoon of yogurt.
look.prompt: For each plate, find a grain, a protein and a vegetable. What nutrient do the black beans and the lentils both give?

check.q: What is dal?
choices: A kind of noodle from Japan
A warm stew of lentils and spices from India
check.why: The reading says dal is a warm stew of lentils cooked with spices, common in India.

check.q: What do beans give in a rice-and-beans meal?
check.why: The reading says the rice gives carbohydrates and the beans give protein and fiber.

check.q: What does fish give the body?
check.why: The reading says fish gives protein and healthy fats.

lessons.title: Breakfast and Balance
lessons.mainIdea: Breakfast refuels the body for learning, and no single food is 'bad'; balance and variety over the day matter most.
reading: You have not eaten all night. In the morning, your body needs fuel. *Breakfast* breaks that overnight fast. Many students find a good breakfast helps them focus and feel steady in class.

Breakfast can look many ways. Oatmeal with fruit. Eggs and a tortilla. Rice with an egg on top. Yogurt and a banana. Many schools serve free or low-cost breakfast too. A mix of a grain, a protein and a fruit gives lasting energy.

No single food is 'bad.' A piece of birthday cake at a party is fine. What matters is the whole day and the whole week. Eating many kinds of foods is called *variety*. If you have questions about food and your body, ask a parent, school nurse or doctor.

words.d: the first meal of the day, which breaks the overnight fast
eating many different kinds of foods

look.title: Build a Breakfast
look.text: Here are some foods: oatmeal, eggs, tortillas, rice, yogurt, milk, bananas, berries, peanut butter, whole-wheat toast, beans and an orange.
look.prompt: Build two different breakfasts. Each should have a grain, a protein and a fruit. Which one would you like best?

check.q: Why is the first meal called breakfast?
choices: It is eaten at school only
check.why: The reading says breakfast breaks the overnight fast after a night without food.

check.q: What does the lesson say about foods like birthday cake?
choices: No single food is 'bad'; the whole day and week matter
check.why: The lesson says no single food is 'bad.' Balance and variety over time matter most.

check.q: What is variety?
choices: Eating many different kinds of foods
check.why: The reading defines variety as eating many kinds of foods.

review.q: Which of these is one of the six main nutrients?
review.why: The six nutrients are carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.

review.q: Which nutrient is the body's main fuel?
review.why: Carbohydrates, in grains, fruit and beans, are the body's main fuel.

review.q: What did James Lind's test with sailors show?
choices: Oranges and lemons helped sailors with scurvy
review.why: Lind found that sailors who ate oranges and lemons got better. We now know these have vitamin C.

review.q: On MyPlate, what fills half the plate?
review.why: MyPlate shows fruits and vegetables filling half the plate.

review.q: On a Nutrition Facts label, what should you look at first?
review.why: The serving size tells you the amount all the other numbers describe.

review.q: How is lentil dal like rice and beans?
choices: Both give protein from plant foods
review.why: Lentils and beans are both plant foods in the bean family that give protein and fiber.

review.q: Which habit helps protect teeth from cavities?
choices: Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste
review.why: Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste makes enamel stronger and helps prevent cavities.

review.q: What is the big idea of healthy eating in this chapter?
choices: Some foods are bad and must never be eaten
Only one country eats healthy food
Balance and variety over the day and week
review.why: The chapter teaches that no food is 'bad' and that balance and variety matter most.
